                    <title>27 exoplanet targets for the world's first private space telescope</title>
                    <description>The Lazuli Space Telescope will be the first private space telescope. It's the brainchild of Eric Schmidt, Google's former CEO. It will have a 3-meter mirror (9.8 feet), larger than Hubble's 2.4-meter mirror (7.9 feet), and will be launched by 2029.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-exoplanet-world-private-space-telescope.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>New binary gene expression system enables independent control of multiple cell types</title>
                    <description>Our bodies are composed of many different types of cells that work together to build and maintain normal physiological functions. In the central nervous system, for example, neurons transmit information, while glial cells such as astrocytes regulate the environment surrounding neurons and support their function. Understanding how these cell types influence one another is essential for uncovering how our bodies develop and function.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-binary-gene-enables-independent-multiple.html</link>
                    <category>Cell & Microbiology</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 20:00:01 EDT</pubDate>

                            <item>
                    <title>Drought forces livestock farmers to make tough decisions: Our model shows the impact on inequality</title>
                    <description>Climate change is amplifying extreme weather conditions across southern Africa. Dry seasons are getting hotter and drier, while rains are becoming heavier and more concentrated. This means greater swings between production surplus and scarcity for rural communities that make their living from the land.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-drought-livestock-farmers-tough-decisions.html</link>

                    <title>South Africa's lion-petting industry: We spent three years investigating and here's what we found</title>
                    <description>An estimated 8,000 lions are held in captivity in South Africa in about 350 places, ranging from zoos to tourism venues where people can interact up close with the big cats. Lions are also bred for live trade, trade in body parts and captive hunts.</description>

                            <item>
                    <title>Inside the narcissistic brain: fMRI research sheds light on the narcissist's struggle with empathy</title>
                    <description>Many people have narcissistic traits to some degree, for example, confidence in one's own superiority, a sense of entitlement and a desire to be the center of attention. However, some people have notably higher levels of narcissistic traits than others, and the neural basis of so-called "grandiose narcissism" has rarely been studied in socially complex situations.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-narcissistic-brain-fmri-narcissist-struggle.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>Water into fuel: The new nanomaterial that could upgrade green hydrogen</title>
                    <description>Generating hydrogen without releasing carbon dioxide sounds simple: pass electricity through water, split water molecules and generate green hydrogen. The hard part is the electrocatalyst. The best ones rely on platinum, ruthenium and iridium, which are scarce and expensive. We wanted to know whether a small amount of iron and nickel oxides, anchored on carbon nanofibers grown by chemical vapor deposition the right way on the right scaffold, could do the job instead. Our results are published in ACS Applied Nano Materials.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-fuel-nanomaterial-green-hydrogen.html</link>
                    <category>Nanomaterials</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 19:00:03 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>Glowing ghoul or chemical tool? The toxic chemistry behind Victorian séances</title>
                    <description>In November 1857, during a séance in Jersey City, the medium Leah Brown claimed her body produced luminous particles. So intense was the luminosity emanating from her, she recalled in her memoir, that it almost burned her hands. She rinsed her hands under a tap and then pushed them into the damp earth outside.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ghoul-chemical-tool-toxic-chemistry.html</link>

                    <title>Spending in‑person time with friends is the biggest predictor of whether college students flourish</title>
                    <description>Exercise, avoiding alcohol or even getting enough sleep aren't the factors most connected to college students' well-being. Spending face-to-face time with friends and other people is the strongest predictor of their mental health, according to a 2026 study of nearly 80,000 students that I conducted with the help of my students.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-inperson-friends-biggest-predictor-college.html</link>
                    <category>Social Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 18:30:01 EDT</pubDate>

                    <description>Ongoing research is providing a clearer picture of how climate change can affect different aspects of the Coorong in South Australia—and is helping develop strong environmental strategies that can be adapted as the climate changes.</description>

                            <item>
                    <title>Could ecological roles offer clues to how life began?</title>
                    <description>Producers, consumers, and decomposers play different roles in today's ecosystems. Thinking about these familiar roles led me to a question: Could their differences partly reflect the different physical and chemical environments in which early life developed? I wondered whether the organization of ecosystems might offer a useful starting point for thinking about life's beginnings.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ecological-roles-clues-life-began.html</link>
                    <category>Ecology</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:40:16 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>Expanding hemp could boost Kentucky water quality and ecological diversity</title>
                    <description>Hemp has long been pitched to Kentucky farmers as a way to diversify their income. Research now suggests it could diversify the landscape itself, with measurable benefits for the state's water and wildlife.</description>

                            <item>
                    <title>Metalens microscope switches focus with voltage, not moving optics</title>
                    <description>Just as it is difficult for a camera to keep both a nearby flower and a distant mountain sharply focused at the same time, conventional optical microscopes face a similar challenge when imaging structures located at different depths inside the body. Tighter focusing of light improves spatial resolution, but at the same time reduces the depth range over which the image remains sharply focused.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-metalens-microscope-focus-voltage-optics.html</link>
                    <category>Optics & Photonics</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:20:10 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>Beyond trial and error: Integrating computation, processing, and AI to design high-entropy alloys</title>
                    <description>Designing structural high-entropy alloys (SHEAs) means solving a problem with an enormous number of moving parts: which combinations of composition and processing conditions will yield the phases, microstructures, and mechanical properties a given application demands? Because these alloys mix multiple principal elements in comparable proportions, that question spans length and time scales that no single experiment or model can cover on its own.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-trial-error-ai-high-entropy.html</link>
                    <category>Materials Science</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 17:20:01 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>Silent bacterial genes yield potential leads for future cancer drugs</title>
                    <description>Natural products produced by microorganisms are a promising source of new drugs. Researchers at the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) and its Saarbrücken-based site, the Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS), have now discovered a new family of such compounds, elucidated their unusual biosynthesis and developed a way to produce them synthetically.</description>

                    <title>Light-based monitoring could improve quality checks for lab-grown replacement cartilage</title>
                    <description>A new doctoral dissertation by Omar Anwar Elkadi in the field of Applied Physics on near-infrared spectroscopy for the continuous monitoring of tissue-engineered cartilage will be defended at the  Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Kuopio campus, of the University of Eastern Finland on Oct. 30.</description>

                            <item>
                    <title>Can cats really thrive on vegan diets? Professor Andrew Knight responds to critics</title>
                    <description>In response to a recent article on vegan diets for cats, Phys.org received numerous messages from concerned readers. People raised a lot of concerns, mainly arguing that cats are obligate carnivores and that vegan diets could be very harmful to their health. Now, we have collected all these comments, questions and concerns and asked the researcher behind the original paper to address them. Andrew Knight, Veterinary Professor of Animal Welfare and Associate Professor at Murdoch University School of Veterinary Medicine, offers his response below.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-cats-vegan-diets-professor-andrew.html</link>

                    <title>Aleppo pine at risk: Climate impacts arrive decades earlier than projected</title>
                    <description>In 2020, our research published in New Phytologist showed how the height growth of Aleppo pine populations responded to climate gradients across the Mediterranean, and how these populations were expected to respond under future climate change based on decades of common-garden experiments. Since then, multiple studies on Pinus halepensis have documented diverse and often rapid growth and survival responses to recent climatic extremes.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-aleppo-climate-impacts-decades-earlier.html</link>

                    <title>Single optical element combines soft X-ray imaging and spectroscopy</title>
                    <description>An international research team from Germany, Switzerland and Japan has demonstrated in a recent study that a single reflection zone plate (RZP) can perform both soft X-ray imaging and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) mapping. The approach could simplify future instruments that need to determine both where structures are located in a material and how their electronic properties vary.</description>

                    <title>Simulations reveal design rules for high-performance DNA particle motors</title>
                    <description>DNA-nano/microparticle motors are among the fastest artificial molecular motors reported to date, moving at approximately 30 nm per second.                     <title>Shared aquifers, border hotspots: Cooperation should follow where groundwater is pumped, scientists say</title>
                    <description>Groundwater depletion and groundwater-dependent irrigation tend to concentrate close to international borders within aquifers shared by two or more countries, where pumping on one side is more likely to affect users on the other, according to a publication by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH).</description>

                    <title>Hidden chromosome structures reveal greater complexity in how roundworms organize DNA</title>
                    <description>Almost every cell in our body contains around two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, packed into a tiny nucleus. Yet for the cell to function, this enormous amount of genetic material must remain organized and accessible. Researchers at the University of Basel have now discovered three distinct types of large chromosomal domains that help organize DNA in nuclei.</description>
